text: Your new desk neighbor Fyodor shakes your hand and immediately asks: “Got a charger? I’ll give it back by lunch, I swear.”
Fyodor is moving: “Just twenty boxes and a piano. Saturday, 8 a.m. Pizza’s on me!”
Fyodor brings his cat Bagel to the office: “No pets allowed in my rental. Can he hang out under your desk? He’s quiet.”
left: Under my desk is for feet

text: Fyodor’s apartment fell through again — second move in six months. “Same boxes, same piano. You know the way!”
left: I do. That’s why it’s a no

text: The Boss is heading for your desk. Fyodor whispers from under it: “Say I’m in a meeting. Bagel has a video call with the vet.”
left: He’s under the desk, right here

text: Six months later, Fyodor returns your charger: wrapped in electrical tape, labeled “Bagel,” and somehow with a different plug.
Fyodor is visiting his parents: “Can you keep Bagel for a week? He only eats duck pâté and only sleeps on laptops.”
Fyodor bought an apartment! The last move ever, he swears. Housewarming on Friday, and you’re on the “closest people” list.
right: I’ll bring a charger as a gift

text: The Boss wants someone to blame for the blown report. Fyodor stands up: “That was me. Bagel and I will redo it all by morning.”
Fyodor is moving to another desk and taking your monitor, your chair and, apparently, your charger. “I needed them more.”
Alexei, the office optimizer, sends a “quick intro” deck: forty slides. Slide 1: “Who I am.” Slide 40: “Who you are.”
Alexei rolls out “Kanban for Lunch”: a board on the fridge reading “Want” — “Heating” — “Eating.” Your soup is stuck in “Heating.”
Alexei asks you to log what you’re doing in his spreadsheet every 15 minutes. “It only takes 15 minutes an hour!”
Alexei rehearses his presentation for the Boss in front of you. Forty slides, twelve charts, one joke on slide 37.
“Kanban for Lunch” has grown: the microwave line now has sprints and retros. Alexei wants you as Lunch Scrum Master.
The Boss opened Alexei’s spreadsheet and has been silent for three minutes. Alexei whispers: “Say the formulas were your idea.”
The Boss loves Alexei’s spreadsheet. The whole department fills it in, it has 48 tabs, and yours is red.
Year in review. Alexei is preparing “What We Optimized” and wants your photo on slide 40, captioned “Engine of Process.”
left: Ask him to drop the photo

text: The Boss wants a report by morning. Alexei sends a file: “I made a template for your tasks in advance. Forty tabs, all calculated.”
Alexei launched the “Transparency” process: your late arrivals are now highlighted in the shared spreadsheet. In red. Animated.
right: Invite him for a peace coffee

text: Robert, in a curly ’80s wig: “Back to the ’80s office party! The committee is one person short. Guess who?”
left: I really need to finish a report

text: Robert holds out an envelope: “We’re chipping in for a gift for Viktor Sergeyevich!” Not even Robert knows who Viktor Sergeyevich is.
Karaoke at the team-building. Robert, already in the wig, hands you the second mic: “Duet! ‘Total Eclipse of the Heart’! The people demand it!”
Robert, carrying a box: “Costume contest! We need glitter glued onto thirty wigs. Lunch is overrated anyway, right?”
Robert ordered one cake for all of the quarter’s birthdays. It’s the size of a desk, and it has to go past the Boss’s office.
It’s Robert’s birthday, and there’s nobody to collect money for his gift — that’s usually his job. He stares sadly at an empty envelope.
New Year’s party. Host Robert’s wig just ripped, and he’s on in two minutes. “You’re my co-host, right? Say yes!”
A year has passed. Robert solemnly takes off his ’80s wig and hands it to you: “The next party is yours. I believe in you!”
The Boss is hunting for whoever blew the deadline. Robert bursts in wearing the wig: “Surprise karaoke!” — and the Boss is already belting out “Don’t Stop Believin’.”
Robert is offended. In the team chat: “Responsible for all gift collections until the end of the year — you! Envelope’s on your desk.”
Galya perches on the edge of your desk: “Let’s trade: you give me one piece of news, I give you two. Strictly confidential. Confidential to everyone.”
Galya narrows her eyes: “Someone’s secretly washing all the shared mugs. Is it you? Confess, I won’t tell anyone! Well, hardly anyone.”
Galya is investigating “Who’s eating other people’s yogurts” and asks you to keep lookout by the kitchen. Forty minutes. Maybe an hour.
Galya whispers: “There’s a rumor Oleg wants you in his department. Should I deny it? Or let everyone know — it’s so exciting!”
The rumor about you has grown: now they say you’re joining the space program. Galya: “I can stop it. But I need fresh news.”
right: Spill the news about the cake

text: Galya launched the “Galya Gazette” in the team chat and wants you to run the “Yogurt of the Week” column. Every Monday. No breaks.
Galya is upset: she was the last to hear about the desk reshuffle. “Tell me anything! Even about the stapler!”
A year has passed. Galya admits she started that rumor about you herself, and is preparing a final issue: “Colleague of the Year — confidential to everyone!”
Galya whispers: “Just between us: tomorrow the Boss will ask about the report you haven’t started. I didn’t say anything.”
Office rumor: you love overtime. Galya “accidentally” said it in front of the Boss, and he happily signed you up for Saturday.
Oleg from the next department texts: “Cover for me, I’m in the elevator!” His location says the elevator is coming from two towns over. The manager asks where Oleg is.
Oleg shows off his project “ParkOleg” — an app for finding parking near the office. He wants you to test it over lunch: “You’re the first user! Well, after my mom.”
Oleg dumps his part of the report on you: “It’s five minutes of work, and I have a dentist.” The report is thirty pages. It’s his third dentist this month.
left: Hand it back with a smile

text: Oleg is an hour late but brought you a latte. His story for the manager: “A duck and her ducklings were crossing the road, so I escorted them.” He needs a witness.
Oleg invites you to pitch “ParkOleg” to investors on Saturday: “You’ll be CTO. Just stand confidently and nod at the word ‘blockchain.’”
right: Put on a blazer and nod

text: The manager put you and Oleg on a joint project. Oleg vanished for a week “at a hackathon.” Two days to the deadline, and his part is an empty file named “final_for_real.”
Oleg is late for his own annual review. He whispers into the phone: “Start without me, you know me best. Just don’t mention the ducks.”
“ParkOleg” has launched! Twelve users, eleven of them Oleg’s mom. He offers you one percent of the company for helping out on weekends.
The manager is looking for whoever missed the deadline. Oleg stands up: “That was me. Late, as usual.” For the first time all year he covers for you — and winks.
Oleg at the stand-up: “The report is late because somebody didn’t cover for me.” Everyone looks at you. The manager slowly raises an eyebrow.
Marina Petrovna from accounting looks over her glasses: “New here? Expense reports are due by the fifth. Not the sixth. The fifth.” You suddenly want to report everything, even what you never spent.
right: Write it down in three places

text: After your business trip, the hotel receipt stayed in your jacket pocket. The jacket is at the dry cleaner’s. Marina Petrovna wants the original and doesn’t believe in dry cleaners.
left: “Can we do it without a receipt?”
right: Ask the hotel for a copy

text: Marina Petrovna is off to a seminar and, for the first time, asks a personal favor: water the violets on her windowsill. “Strictly on schedule. Like a tax return.”
The fifth, 5:55 p.m. Your expense report isn’t ready. Accounting closes at 6:00. Sharp. Marina Petrovna is already putting on her coat.
Marina Petrovna found a pet store receipt in your report: “Hamster food, 2 kg.” You mixed up the receipts. She’s been silent for a full minute.
Marina Petrovna whispers the news: her “Summer Twilight” violet has bloomed. She shows you forty photos. Each with commentary. Your lunch break is melting away.
Year end. Marina Petrovna is closing the quarter and asks you to sort six hundred receipts by date: “You’re a tidy person, I’ve noticed. Don’t argue.”
Marina Petrovna gives you a violet cutting: “Water once a week. Growth report due by the fifth.” It seems to be a joke. It seems.
The manager is fuming: your travel report has “gone missing.” Marina Petrovna silently pulls it from the safe: “Received on the fourth. Ahead of schedule.”
Marina Petrovna returns your expense report for the seventh time: the paperclip is on the wrong side. Your travel money has been stuck for two months.
left: Redo it and bring a violet
